title: In 1,000+ Kids Who Claimed to Have Past Lives, Their 'Reincarnation' Came 12 Months After a Sudden Death
excerpt: And scientists can’t explain the creepy correlation.
content:
Shawn Gorman

Wed, October 21, 2026 at 7:11 PM UTC

Reincarnation isn’t exactly standard fare for peer-reviewed journals. But for more than 60 years, researchers at the University of Virginia’s Division of Perceptual Studies have been building the world’s largest archive of what they call Cases of the Reincarnation Type (CORT)—instances where young children spontaneously report detailed memories that seem to match the life of a specific deceased person.

To understand the archive, you have to look at the spectacular nature of the cases themselves. Take James, a Louisiana toddler who began having violent night terrors about a flaming plane crash. By age three, he told his parents he was a World War II pilot who flew a fighter plane off an aircraft carrier called the Natoma Bay, and he even named a fellow pilot, Jack Larsen. UVA researchers matched his dozens of highly specific claims to a real pilot, James Huston Jr., who was shot down over the Pacific in 1945.

In another famous UVA case, a four-year-old Oklahoma boy named Ryan directed his mother to a 1930s Hollywood promotional photograph, pointed to an uncredited extra, and announced, “That’s me.” He subsequently provided 55 verified, obscure details about the life of deceased Hollywood agent Marty Martyn—including the name of the street he lived on, how many sisters he had, and his favorite food.

Now, a new large-scale analysis of that archive, published in Psychology of Consciousness: Theory, Research, and Practice, has uncovered a statistical oddity that’s puzzling researchers.

The team, led by cognitive neuroscience researcher Saeedeh Sadeghi, analyzed 1,678 cases in which investigators had identified a named “Past Person” whose biographical details matched a child’s statements. Each case had been vetted by investigators interviewing the child, parents, relatives, and neighbors, then cross-checking the claims against verifiable records.

The variable of interest was “intermission time,” which means the time gap between the Past Person’s death and the child’s birth. Across the 1,319 cases with usable timing data, the median intermission was 16 months, although the longest observed intermission time in the dataset was a staggering 150 years.

Now, here’s where the weird science gets really weird. When the Past Person died suddenly—in an accident, by violence (like the World War II pilot), or from an abrupt medical crisis—the intermission time shrank. Completely unexpected deaths were linked to a median gap of just 12 months, compared to 21 months for the most anticipated deaths. That’s a roughly 43 percent reduction, and the more unexpected the death, the shorter the interval.

The obvious counterargument is cultural contamination, since it seems intuitive that families who believe in reincarnation will tend to foster such stories. But the researchers carefully ran moderation analyses for verification quality, memory contamination, family association, social status, and reincarnation belief. Remarkably, they found that the pattern of shortened intermission time was stronger in families whose religions don’t endorse reincarnation at all.

“These results do not support the idea that social beliefs are driving this pattern,” Philip Cozzolino, a social psychologist at UVA, says in a press release.

An interesting detail from the research is that unnatural deaths accounted for 57% of the analyzed cases, while 68% of the deaths were rated as completely unexpected. The researchers noted that this dramatic overrepresentation of unnatural and unexpected deaths far exceeds their prevalence in general mortality statistics. The median age of the “Past Person” at the time of their death was also remarkably young, at just 30 years old

Of course, before we leap to conclusions, it’s important to note that the effect is modest. Death unexpectedness explained only about 2 to 3 percent of the variance in intermission time, and the data are purely observational. So it’s possible that subjective factors lie behind this strange data anomaly, and the results don’t prove that consciousness survives death.

What makes the data noteworthy, the researchers argue, is that any link exists at all, since no conventional mechanism connects how someone died to when an unrelated child is born. Intriguingly, the pattern echoes beliefs found in Hindu, Buddhist, and Indigenous North American traditions, where sudden death is thought to leave unfinished business that hastens rebirth.

“Is this evidence of anything metaphysical? The data are observational and we’re careful to stay agnostic about mechanism,” Sadeghi says in the press release. “What I can say is that the pattern is real in the data ... which, to me, is a reason to keep looking, not to look away.”
